name: MARIGLIA
description: Mariglia is a four-player partnership trick-taking game from Sardinia, Italy, particularly popular in the North around Sassari, Olbia, and Nuoro. Known as 'Bridge Sardo' (Sardinian Bridge) for its strategic depth, it belongs to the Manille family where the Seven is the highest and most valuable card. The game allows open communication between partners, making it unique among trick-taking games.

content.text: Mariglia is a four-player partnership trick-taking game from Sardinia, Italy, particularly popular in the North around Sassari, Olbia, and Nuoro. Known as 'Bridge Sardo' (Sardinian Bridge) for its strategic depth, it belongs to the Manille family where the Seven is the highest and most valuable card. The game allows open communication between partners, making it unique among trick-taking games.
A Sardinian variant of the Manille family of games, sharing etymology with Manille, Manillen, Malilla, and similar European games where a specific card (the Seven) holds special value.
4 players in two fixed partnerships, partners sitting opposite each other. Deal and play are anticlockwise.

40-card Italian deck of the French-suited Genoese pattern. Ranking: 7 (Mariglia) > Ace > King > Jack > Queen > 6 > 5 > 4 > 3 > 2. Note: Jack ranks higher than Queen (as in Portugal and Southern Italy).

First dealer chosen by drawing cards (lowest deals). Turn to deal passes to the right. Dealer shuffles, player to left cuts (minimum 5 cards each portion). Deal anticlockwise in packets of 5 cards (two rounds), 10 cards each. Bottom card (dealer's last card) indicates trumps (il trionfo) and is placed face up.

items.text: Target score: Common targets are 35 or 45 game points; sometimes 70 or 71 for a single long game. Match may be best of three games to 45, or first two to 35 then deciding game to 45.
Exposure of cards when dealing: Some play that dealer may expose the bottom card (trump) before dealing, and may expose cards from certain packets; tournament rules forbid exposure during the deal.

Communication rules: Local conventions vary: sometimes only the team currently winning the trick may speak; some require yes/no or numeric answers only; some allow concealing holding the mariglia of trumps when asked.
